name: EASTL hash_map / hash_set (eastl::hash_map)
workload: Stopwatch (CPU cycles) comparison of eastl::hash_map against the compiler-supplied hash map on 10,000 random pairs with keys drawn from [0,5000), for uint32_t->TestObject and string->uint32_t (same FNV-style string hash for both), timing insert, find, operator[], count, erase, iteration and clear.
claimed_speedup: EASTL 0.96 release table vs the compiler-supplied hash map (ratio = other time / EASTL time, above 1 means EASTL faster). hash_map<uint32_t,TestObject>: find 1.55x, insert 1.64x, operator[] 1.21x, count 2.51x, erase val 1.54x, erase range 5.26x. hash_map<string,uint32_t>: find 3.26x, find_as/char* 3.70x, insert 1.24x, operator[] 3.10x, count 3.77x, iteration 3.67x. Slower: clear 0.53x (uint32 key) and 0.38x (string key), erase pos 0.79x and 0.56x.
compiler_and_flags: doc/Benchmarks.md: Microsoft Visual C++ 7.1 (version 1310), Release 'full optimization, inlining enabled' (exact flags not given), allocator PPMalloc::GeneralAllocator with thread safety. N2271 Linux column: GCC 4.1 -O3 with libstdc++; Windows column: VC8 -Og -Oi -Ot -Oy -Ob2 -GF -Gy.
hardware: doc/Benchmarks.md gives no CPU. N2271 lists Pentium 4 x86 (Windows and Linux columns), a 64-bit PowerPC console and a G5 PowerPC Mac, without exact models.
stars_or_usage: 9.4k stars, 1.0k forks; Electronic Arts' in-house STL replacement, open-sourced
tradeoffs: Node-based separate-chaining table (hashtable.h: prime bucket counts, load-factor rehash policy, optional cached hash code via bCacheHashCode), so it keeps std::unordered_map's pointer and reference stability and its cache behaviour, not an open-addressing layout. Adds find_as and heterogeneous lookup to avoid temporary string keys. The default allocator model needs the application to supply the EASTL operator new[] overloads (name, flags, alignment arguments). Different types from std, so no drop-in interchange with std::unordered_map in APIs.
caveats: The only published tables are doc/Benchmarks.md (EASTL version 0.96.00, Windows x86, Microsoft Visual C++ 7.1 with the Dinkumware STL or STLport, custom PPMalloc allocator, no CPU model stated) and the 2007 WG21 paper N2271 (doc/EASTL-n2271.pdf, written by EASTL's author). They are roughly 20 years old and predate std::unordered_map in those compilers' libraries. Ratios are other-STL time divided by EASTL time from a single stopwatch run in CPU cycles, with no variance reported. Mixed result, not a clear win: the N2271 Linux column (Pentium 4, GCC 4.1 -O3, libstdc++) shows uint32-key find 0.76x, insert 0.91x, operator[] 1.37x, and string-key find 0.75x, insert 3.52x, operator[] 3.00x, so EASTL was slower than libstdc++ on find. The current benchmark/source/BenchmarkHash.cpp targets std::unordered_map, but its results are not published, and its tables are tiny (10,000 elements) and cache-resident. The repo has no absl::flat_hash_map or folly F14 comparison at all, and EASTL's chained design is expected to trail those flat maps; that was not measured. Martin Ankerl's hashmap benchmark pages could not be opened here (host blocked), so no third-party figure was verified. The library-wide claim in doc/Design.md and doc/FAQ.md that 'EASTL is faster than all existing STL implementations' is not supported by these tables for this facility. hash_set has no separate numbers; the record covers hash_map.

name: EASTL string (eastl::basic_string / eastl::string, eastl::fixed_string)
workload: Stopwatch (CPU cycles) comparison of eastl::basic_string against std::basic_string for 8-bit and char16_t strings, both pre-sized to 16 characters so initial reserve differences are removed, timing push_back, insert, erase, replace, reserve, operator[], the find family, compare, swap and iteration.
claimed_speedup: EASTL 0.96 release table vs VC++ 7.1 (Dinkumware) std::basic_string (ratio = std time / EASTL time, above 1 means EASTL faster). string<char8_t>: push_back 10.41x, reserve 10.73x, swap 3.48x, operator[] 2.61x, find_first_of 2.23x, find_last_of 1.60x, rfind 1.32x. string<char16_t>: push_back 14.30x, reserve 4.87x, swap 3.48x, operator[] 2.98x, find 2.43x, compare 1.73x. Slower: char8_t find 0.74x and compare 0.82x. About 1.0x for erase, insert, replace, iteration and size.
compiler_and_flags: doc/Benchmarks.md: Microsoft Visual C++ 7.1 (version 1310), Release 'full optimization, inlining enabled' (exact flags not given), PPMalloc::GeneralAllocator. N2271 Linux column: GCC 4.1 -O3 with libstdc++.
hardware: doc/Benchmarks.md gives no CPU. N2271 lists Pentium 4 x86 for the Windows and Linux columns, without an exact model.
stars_or_usage: 9.4k stars, 1.0k forks; Electronic Arts' in-house STL replacement, open-sourced
tradeoffs: Current string.h implements the short string optimization inside the 3-pointer object: capacity (sizeof(HeapLayout)-1)/sizeof(char), i.e. 23 chars on 64-bit. Non-copy-on-write. The allocator is an instance member with a debug name, not a template argument of the type, so strings with different allocators share one type. eastl::fixed_string<T, N, bEnableOverflow=true> keeps N characters inline and falls back to the heap if allowed. A different type from std::string, so conversions at API boundaries copy. The default allocator needs the application to supply EASTL's operator new[] overloads.
caveats: The only published tables are doc/Benchmarks.md (EASTL version 0.96.00, Windows x86, Microsoft Visual C++ 7.1 with the Dinkumware STL or STLport, custom PPMalloc allocator, no CPU model stated) and the 2007 WG21 paper N2271 (doc/EASTL-n2271.pdf, written by EASTL's author). They are roughly 20 years old and predate std::unordered_map in those compilers' libraries. Ratios are other-STL time divided by EASTL time from a single stopwatch run in CPU cycles, with no variance reported. The tables are EASTL version 0.96.00; the current include/EASTL/string.h has the SSO layout above, so the published rows may not describe today's code, and the harness pre-sizes strings to 16 characters, so the SSO benefit is not what the rows measure. The baseline in the Windows tables is the 2005 Dinkumware string, and in N2271's Linux column it is the copy-on-write std::string of libstdc++ 4.1 (GCC 4.1 -O3), neither of which is a modern libstdc++ new-ABI, libc++ or current MSVC string, so the speedups are probably much smaller today. N2271 Linux column (Pentium 4, GCC 4.1 -O3): char8_t push_back 2.28x, find 5.06x, find_first_of 10.11x, rfind 8.70x, insert 0.77x; reserve rows show a ratio of exactly 100.00, which looks like a cap in the ratio output. char8_t in the benchmark source is EABase's 8-bit char typedef (the suite does not compile with C++20 char8_t, see benchmark/CMakeLists.txt). No comparison against folly fbstring exists in the repo.

name: EASTL sort algorithms (eastl::sort / quick_sort, eastl::radix_sort)
workload: Stopwatch (CPU cycles) comparison of eastl::quick_sort (what eastl::sort maps to) against std::sort on arrays and vectors of about 10,000 uint32_t, 8-byte ValuePair and TestObject elements, for random input and for already-sorted input.
claimed_speedup: EASTL 0.96 release table, quick_sort vs VC++ 7.1 (Dinkumware) std::sort (ratio = std time / EASTL time, above 1 means EASTL faster). Random input: vector<uint32> 1.87x, vector<ValuePair> 1.84x, vector<TestObject> 1.78x, TestObject[] 1.72x. Already-sorted input: vector<uint32> 1.28x, vector<ValuePair> 1.25x, but vector<TestObject> 0.55x and TestObject[] 0.59x (EASTL slower). vector<uint64>/sort 1.02x. No radix_sort or std::stable_sort numbers are published.
compiler_and_flags: doc/Benchmarks.md: Microsoft Visual C++ 7.1 (version 1310), Release 'full optimization, inlining enabled' (exact flags not given). N2271 Linux column: GCC 4.1 -O3 with libstdc++.
hardware: doc/Benchmarks.md gives no CPU. N2271 lists Pentium 4 x86 for the Windows and Linux columns, without an exact model.
stars_or_usage: 9.4k stars, 1.0k forks; Electronic Arts' in-house STL replacement, open-sourced
tradeoffs: eastl::sort maps to quick_sort, an unstable introsort needing random-access iterators; eastl::stable_sort maps to merge_sort. eastl::radix_sort is an LSD radix sort for integral keys only: elements need a radix_type key (or a key-extractor functor), it is stable, and it needs a caller-supplied scratch buffer as large as the input. The benchmark source notes it performs poorly on contiguous ordered keys (kOrdered).
caveats: The only published tables are doc/Benchmarks.md (EASTL version 0.96.00, Windows x86, Microsoft Visual C++ 7.1 with the Dinkumware STL or STLport, custom PPMalloc allocator, no CPU model stated) and the 2007 WG21 paper N2271 (doc/EASTL-n2271.pdf, written by EASTL's author). They are roughly 20 years old and predate std::unordered_map in those compilers' libraries. Ratios are other-STL time divided by EASTL time from a single stopwatch run in CPU cycles, with no variance reported. N2271 Linux column (Pentium 4, GCC 4.1 -O3, libstdc++): quick_sort ratios range from 0.96x (vector<uint32> random) to 1.34x (vector<TestObject> sorted), so against libstdc++'s sort the gain was small. The std::sort implementations of 2005-2007 are far behind current libstdc++, libc++ and MSVC introsorts, so the 1.7-1.9x does not transfer. radix_sort: include/EASTL/sort.h only says it is 'typically faster than any other sort' for integral data (qualitative). The current benchmark/source/BenchmarkSort.cpp compares radix_sort, tim_sort, merge_sort, heap_sort and eastl::sort against std::sort and std::stable_sort at sizes 10 to 10000 over random, random-sorted, ordered and mostly-ordered uint32_t input, but it prints its tables at run time and no results are checked in, and no independent radix_sort measurement was found (one WebSearch, nothing about EASTL). eastl::copy is in the same family: Benchmarks.md release rows give algorithm/copy/vector<LargePOD> 1.30x and copy/vector<uint32_t> 0.91x (EASTL slower), so no copy win is claimed.

name: ETL static containers (etl::vector, etl::map, etl::unordered_map)
baseline: std::unordered_map (the only container with a timing harness); also std::vector and std::map
workload: No published measurement. The repo's test/Performance/unordered_map program times 16 rounds of inserting then erasing 10,000,000 sequential uint64_t->uint16_t entries in std::unordered_map and in etl::unordered_map sized for 10,000,000 entries, printing milliseconds for each, but no results are recorded anywhere in the repo or docs.
claimed_speedup: None stated. No numbers in the README, the docs or test/Performance; the README only says the containers give 'predictability, performance, and memory control' and 'cache efficiency' through contiguous storage.
tradeoffs: Fixed capacity set at compile time and no heap use at all: no malloc, no new, deterministic latency, contiguous storage, memory fully known at build time. Cost: a container cannot grow past its template capacity (overflow goes to the configured ETL error handler or assert), and etl::unordered_map<K,V,MAX_SIZE,MAX_BUCKETS> reserves its whole node pool and bucket array up front. Size-independent i-prefixed base types (ivector, iunordered_map) allow size-erased use. Supports C++03 upward and does not depend on the STL.
caveats: Tier D: the project does not claim to be faster than the std containers; its stated goals are determinism and heap-free operation for embedded targets. A Windows-only timing harness exists (QueryPerformanceCounter, Visual Studio project): https://github.com/ETLCPP/etl/blob/master/test/Performance/unordered_map/unordered_map/unordered_map.cpp, but it ships no results, flags or hardware, so running it is the way to get tier A evidence. Where ETL is faster, the likely cause is avoided heap allocation, which a fixed-capacity container gets by construction; a std::vector with reserve() or a pooled allocator would narrow the gap. Searched the README, docs/containers, docs/blog and test/Performance, plus two WebSearch queries for independent ETL-vs-std timings; none found. The etlcpp.com site was not opened.

name: ETL fixed-capacity strings and algorithms (etl::string, etl::algorithm)
workload: No published measurement for strings or for the algorithm and sort functions; nothing was found in the README, docs/strings, docs/utilities or the test tree.
claimed_speedup: None stated. The docs describe etl::string as a fixed-capacity string with a truncation flag and etl::algorithm as STL-style algorithm implementations, with no speed claim.
tradeoffs: etl::string<N> keeps N characters in the object with no heap; text that would exceed capacity is truncated and an internal truncated flag is set (or an error is asserted if ETL_STRING_TRUNCATION_IS_ERROR is defined). It is a distinct type from std::string, and the algorithm functions exist mainly so that code can run without the STL header set (C++03 backports and extra helpers).
caveats: Tier D: no numbers anywhere, and no sign that the author claims a speed win; the value is heap-free, predictable-latency strings. The baselines named in the assignment (std::string, std::sort) have no ETL timing. docs/utilities/algorithms.md lists the functions and says nothing about speed. Kept as a placeholder record in case a user benchmark appears; the container record for the same repo has the only existing timing harness (test/Performance/unordered_map, no results). Two WebSearch queries for independent ETL timings found nothing.

name: rpp (TheNumbat/rpp) compile-time-oriented containers and allocators
baseline: std::vector, std::unordered_map and the other STL container headers (MSVC STL)
workload: Author's anecdotal whole-project comparison: an earlier STL-based project against a rendering project of about 100k lines written on rpp, compared by frontend compile time per translation unit.
claimed_speedup: Slowest translation unit about 10 s in the compiler frontend for the STL-based project vs 1.4 s with rpp (about 7x, derived from page data); including rpp's core header costs under 200 ms per translation unit on average; the optimized build of the roughly 100k-line project finishes in under 3 s.
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in STL: Rust-inspired own API (Vec, Map, String, Box, Rc, Opt, Region allocators with statically associated allocators), explicit code, no STL or system headers pulled in, about 10k lines. Supports only MSVC 19.39+ on x64 and Clang 17+ on x64 and aarch64 (GCC not supported); uses GCC/Clang vector extensions for SIMD; C++20 required.
caveats: Snippet only: thenumb.at could not be opened (EGRESS_BLOCKED, DNS failure on two tries), so the figures come from a WebSearch result summary of the 'Oxidizing C++' post, which also quotes the author saying it is not a proper benchmark because it compares two entirely separate codebases. Hardware and compiler (AMD 5950X, MSVC 19.38, Windows 11) come from the same snippet's footnote. Compile-time claim only: the repo README, tree (rpp, test, .github) and the search results contain no runtime benchmark against std::vector, std::unordered_map or std::allocator, so there is no runtime record to separate out. README to-do list admits open performance items (Map still stores hashes of integer keys; Range_Allocator overhead). Last commit is 2024-12-25.
